metaDescription: CO-45 explained: the charge exceeds the fee schedule or contracted amount. Why this is usually a normal write-off, not a denial, and when to check it.
summary: The billed charge was higher than the payer's allowed amount, so the difference is written off as a contractual adjustment.
causes: Your billed charge is above the payer's fee schedule or contract rate
The payer paid the allowed amount, which is normal for an in-network claim
A rare cause: the fee schedule or contract rate on file is out of date
fixes: For most claims, post the adjustment as a contractual write-off and move on
Compare the allowed amount to your contract; if it is lower than agreed, treat it as an underpayment and dispute it
Do not bill the patient for the CO-45 amount when you are in network
prevention: Keep contract rates loaded in your billing system
Review payments against expected amounts so underpayments surface early

faqs.question: Is CO-45 a denial?
faqs.answer: Usually no. It is a routine contractual adjustment on a paid claim. It only becomes a problem if the allowed amount is below your contract.

faqs.question: Can the patient be billed the CO-45 amount?
faqs.answer: Generally not for in-network claims, because the adjustment is a contractual obligation. Check your payer contract and state rules.
